## Organization rules

These apply to every project in this organization. Change them in flicker (`flicker harness rule add --org-wide`), not in this file.


# LogOut — agent instructions

LogOut is a small, public Elixir Hex package (`log_out`, MIT): a pluggable
`:logger` backend that forwards application logs and exceptions to team chat
platforms. It hooks Elixir's native `:logger` via `:gen_event` and dispatches
each event to one or more **adapters** (Zulip, Slack, Discord, Telegram, or a
custom one) using `Task.start/1`, so a slow webhook never blocks a caller.
Library only — no server, no database, no deploy target. Consumers in this
portfolio: **flicker** (Hex, `~> 0.1.4`), **enventory_new** and **skusync**
(both pinned to a git ref on `go9/log_out`). Because it is published on
hex.pm, unknown third parties may also depend on it.

## Dev commands

```bash
mix deps.get
mix test
mix format          # .formatter.exs is checked in
mix docs            # ExDoc; main page is README.md
```

Elixir `~> 1.18`. Runtime deps: `req` only (`~> 0.5.10 or ~> 0.6`) —
**never add HTTPoison/Tesla/httpc**. `ex_doc` is dev-only. There is no demo
app, no `.env`, and no `mix setup` alias — `mix deps.get && mix test` is the
whole loop. Tests avoid live HTTP by passing a stub adapter module that sends
the forwarded level back to the test process (see
`LogOutTest.EchoAdapter` in `test/log_out_test.exs`) — follow that pattern
rather than hitting a real webhook.

## Release

This is a **Hex package, not a deployed service.** Nothing auto-deploys on
push; there is no server and no CI workflow in this repo.

```bash
mix hex.publish      # requires Hex auth; publishing is irreversible-ish
```

Ritual for a release:

1. Bump `version:` in `mix.exs` (single source of truth — there is no
   `@version` module attribute and no `CHANGELOG.md` in this repo yet).
2. Publish with `mix hex.publish`, then tag the commit.
3. Coordinate with consumers. flicker tracks Hex (`~> 0.1.4`), but
   `enventory_new` and `skusync` pin **git refs**, so a Hex release does not
   reach them — their `mix.exs` ref must be bumped separately.

Never publish from an agent session without explicit human approval.

## Durable gotchas (the public API is a contract)

- **Public API surface** — changing or removing any of these breaks consumers:
  - `LogOut` itself (the `:gen_event` backend registered as
    `config :logger, backends: [:console, LogOut]`).
  - `LogOut.Adapter` — the `@callback send_message(log_event :: map(), config
    :: keyword())` behaviour. Third parties implement it; the callback's shape
    is frozen.
  - Adapter helpers used by custom adapters: `LogOut.format_message/1`,
    `LogOut.format_mfa/1`, `LogOut.get_emoji/1`.
  - Built-in adapters `LogOut.Adapters.{Zulip,Slack,Discord,Telegram}`.
  - The `log_event` map shape passed to adapters:
    `%{level: atom, msg: {:string, binary}, meta: map}`.
- **Config keys** live under `config :logger, LogOut, ...` and are read in
  `configure/1`: `:level`, `:levels`, `:adapters`, plus whatever the adapters
  read from the merged config (`:project_name`, and per-adapter `:url`,
  `:bot_email`, `:bot_api_key`, `:stream`, `:topic`, `:bot_token`, `:chat_id`,
  `:message_thread_id`). Adapter config is `Keyword.merge`d **over** the
  top-level config, so per-adapter keys win.
- **`:level` vs `:levels` are different semantics.** `:level` is a *minimum
  threshold* (`Logger.compare_levels/2`). `:levels` is an *exact allowlist* and
  takes precedence when set — it's the only way to forward `:warning` without
  also forwarding `:error`.
- **`:warn` is normalized to `:warning`** before it reaches
  `Logger.compare_levels/2`. This is deliberate: older deps still emit `:warn`,
  and passing it through made Elixir log its own deprecation warning on *every*
  event, flooding the adapters. Do not remove `normalize_level/1`.
- **Config belongs in `config/runtime.exs`**, not `config/prod.exs` — README
  documents this and consumers rely on it. `prod.exs` is evaluated at compile
  time, so `System.get_env/1` returns `nil` and the backend silently no-ops.
- **Adapters fail soft by design.** Each adapter returns `:ok` and skips
  posting when required config is missing (see `LogOut.Adapters.Zulip`), and a
  nonexistent Zulip stream is a warning, not a crash. A logger backend must
  never take down the host app — keep it that way.
- **Known doc drift:** the README documents a `metadata_filter:` option, but
  **no such option is implemented** in `lib/`. Either implement it or correct
  the README; do not assume it works.

## Workflow

- Tracker = **Flicker Tickets** (`flicker` CLI). GitHub is code-only —
  branches, PRs, review. Never file tickets or plans on GitHub.

## Default build stance: minimal-first (ponytail)

Default to the **laziest solution that actually works** — every task, every host, unprompted. "Actually works" is load-bearing: minimal never trades away correctness, tests, or safety.

Ladder, stop at the first rung that holds: needs to exist at all? (YAGNI) → already in the codebase, reuse it → stdlib → native platform feature → already-installed dep → one line → only then minimum new code. Deletion over addition. Fewest files. Shortest working diff — but only *after* understanding the problem end to end (a small diff in the wrong place is a second bug). Bug fix = root cause at the shared function, not a per-caller patch. Non-trivial logic leaves one runnable check behind.

Never simplify away: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, or anything explicitly requested. User wants the full version → build it, no re-arguing.

Planning is not exempt: prefer the smallest ticket/scope that solves the real need, and question whether the work should exist before decomposing it — over-scoping a plan (umbrella epics, speculative child tickets) is the same failure as over-building code.

- **Claude**: enforced via the `ponytail` skill — active every response, **full** by default (`lite`/`ultra` on request; off only on "stop ponytail" / "normal mode"). Skill: `~/.claude/skills/ponytail`.
- **Pi / other hosts**: apply the same stance even without the skill.

## Database architecture

**Postgres for the product apps lives on flicker.** Each app's database is provisioned as a flicker database/branch — see the app's `DATABASE_URL` in its flicker env config. Don't assume a Neon connection string for any product app.

**The flicker control-plane database is on Supabase** (Free, us-east-1, session pooler) — it went Neon → Aiven (2026-07-03, for cost) → Supabase (2026-07-15, for region choice: Aiven Free auto-placed it in us-west, ~67ms from the Fly app in `iad`). **Neon is no longer umbrella infrastructure at all** — the old control-plane project (`johnorlando-umbrella` / `shy-bonus-27235264`) was **deleted 2026-07-25**, and the only Neon left in the portfolio is wutdu's own separate project (still on Fly). Connection/TLS/backup specifics: `projects/flicker/CLAUDE.md`.

> **Legacy / decommissioning:** the per-app Neon projects are **gone** — the last umbrella one was deleted 2026-07-25. (`wutdu` is the exception — it stays on Fly with its own Neon project + Neon Auth, not migrating.) **Any `*.neon.tech` host in a repo's `.env` is dead config, not a working fallback** — re-pull from flicker (below). Watch for the failure mode that hid this for a month: an app left running on the *old* platform after a migration keeps its old DB's compute billable even with zero users, because an idle Ecto pool and Oban's leader heartbeat alone prevent scale-to-zero. **When you migrate a service, destroy the old deployment — don't just stop pointing at it.**

### Local dev DB for a flicker app = a flicker branch, pulled via the CLI

Do not hand-maintain `DATABASE_URL`, and do not point a flicker app at Neon. Use the **flicker CLI** (neon/fly parity) to fork a personal dev branch and stream the `.env`:

```bash
cd ~/Sites/<app>
flicker database set <app>-prod                         # writes flicker.toml
flicker branch create <you>-dev --database <app>-prod    # CoW clone of prod data (repeat for extra DBs, e.g. *-prices-prod)
flicker secrets set DATABASE_URL=<branch-conn> ... --environment dev/<you>
flicker secrets pull                                     # streams dev/<you> -> ./.env (provenance header)
```

The branch's INTERNAL string (`*-rw.<ns>.svc.cluster.local`, `sslmode=disable`) is the in-cluster app path; the PUBLIC string (`<endpoint_id>.db.flickercloud.com`, `sslmode=require`) is what `branch list` returns and the only path reachable from your laptop. Full model: `agent-workflow/projects/flicker/CLAUDE.md` → "flicker CLI", and `flicker` repo `docs/env-secrets-and-connectivity.md`.

### Ecto connection pooling — MANDATORY

Always detect pooler connections and use the correct `prepare` setting in `config/runtime.exs`. Hardcoding `:named` against a pooler causes 8+ second page loads:

```elixir
prepare_setting =
  if database_url =~ ":6543/" or database_url =~ "-pooler" do
    :unnamed   # poolers don't maintain statement caches
  else
    :named     # direct connections only
  end

config :my_app, MyApp.Repo,
  url: database_url,
  prepare: prepare_setting
```

For a new product-app database, provision it on flicker. The `neon-database-setup` skill is now legacy — the control-plane DB is on Supabase and product-app DBs are flicker-hosted; it applies only to wutdu's remaining standalone Neon project.

## Deployment standards

### App hosting is flicker (K8s cell), not Fly

The Phoenix product apps — skusync, enventory-new, goprint-registry, foodfeed — run on **flicker's Kubernetes cell**. **Do not run `fly deploy` or `fly secrets`** for these apps.

CI deploys by building a Docker image, pushing it to GHCR, then telling the flicker API to roll it:

```bash
# CI pattern (GitHub Actions):
#   1. docker/build-push-action → ghcr.io/orlando-umbrella/<repo>:<sha>
#   2. Resolve app ID by slug, then POST /deploy:
APP_ID=$(curl -fsS "https://flickercloud.com/api/v1/apps" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLICKER_TOKEN" \
  | jq -r '.apps[] | select(.slug=="<app-slug>") | .id')
curl --fail-with-body -sS -X POST "https://flickercloud.com/api/v1/apps/$APP_ID/deploy" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLICKER_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"image\":\"ghcr.io/orlando-umbrella/<repo>:<sha>\"}"
```

- `FLICKER_TOKEN` — per-org API token, stored as a GitHub Secret on each repo.
- Migrations run automatically as a K8s init container (`/app/bin/migrate`) before the new code serves.
- For manual redeploy: re-run the latest CI run (`gh run rerun`) or use the flicker UI.

### UI: lantern-ui (no build-time license)

The portfolio's Phoenix apps use **lantern-ui** (`~/Sites/lantern-ui`, MIT, a public Hex/GitHub dependency) — the drop-in replacement for Fluxon. **No license key is required at build or dep time.** This retired the old `FLUXON_LICENSE_KEY` Docker build secret when the apps migrated off Fluxon; don't add it to new repos. Project-level CLAUDE.md should re-state the project's exact flicker app slug so agents don't have to recall it.

### CI/CD pattern: deploys are explicit, on a `deployed` branch

**Merging to `main` ships nothing.** A deploy is a deliberate fast-forward of the repo's deploy branch:

```bash
git push origin origin/main:deployed
```

That push is the only rollout trigger. Tests still run on `pull_request`, so the code reaching `main` has already been proven; the deploy path does not re-run the suite.

This applies to every flicker-hosted app repo (`flicker`, `foodfeed`, `enventory_new`, `skusync`, `goprint-registry`, `agenteye`). The iOS repos use the same model with a differently-named branch — `test-flight`, driven by Xcode Cloud — which is where the pattern came from.

Why it's worth the extra step:
- `deployed` is a **durable record of what is actually in production**. Previously that existed only in Actions run history.
- `git log deployed..main` is exactly the **unreleased set**.
- **Rollback is moving a ref** (`git push -f origin <good-sha>:deployed`), which both restores the invariant and re-runs the pipeline on the known-good commit.
- Merge and deploy stop being the same act, so a broken deploy pipeline no longer blocks merging, and batching work no longer means batching production rollouts.

**Required GitHub Secrets** on each app repo:
- `FLICKER_TOKEN` — flicker per-org API token
  <br>(No `FLUXON_LICENSE_KEY` — the apps use lantern-ui, a public dependency.)

**Merging to `main` needs no deploy approval** — it ships nothing. Confirm before pushing `deployed`; that is the act that reaches production. Leaving `deployed` pointing at a bad SHA is the dangerous state: the next person reads it as "this is live".

### CI minute discipline (GitHub Actions cost)

The org is on the **free** plan (2,000 Actions minutes/month; Linux overage ~$0.008/min). Two rules keep every flicker repo's CI cheap — apply them to **all** of them:

1. **Run the test suite on `pull_request` only — never re-run it on the push to `main`.** Tests gate the *PR*, not the merge: by the time a PR merges it already ran green, and branch-first + rebase-before-merge means the tested code IS what lands. So the test job carries `if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'`, and the `deploy` job does NOT `needs: test` (it runs on the main push, gated only by the fast pre-deploy checks like the migration-prefix check). This kills the redundant test run on every merge.
2. **Don't partition the suite into parallel matrix jobs unless wall-clock genuinely demands it.** Each partition is its own runner that re-pays the full setup tax (deps + compile + DB), so N partitions ≈ **N× the billed minutes** even though wall-clock drops. One `mix test` job is the default; reach for partitions only on a suite slow enough that the minute cost is worth the speed.

Together these roughly **quartered** enventory_new's per-change test spend (4-partition × run-twice → 1 job × run-once).

## Environment variable management

**No Doppler.** Every project uses direct env vars. Local dev = `.env` file (gitignored). For **flicker apps**, stream `.env` from your personal flicker dev environment with `flicker secrets pull` (see Database architecture → "Local dev DB for a flicker app") — don't copy a stale `.env.example` or reuse an old Neon `DATABASE_URL`. Production = the flicker app's env config (set via the flicker API/CLI/UI), **not `fly secrets`**.

### Local

```bash
flicker secrets pull   # flicker apps: stream ./.env from dev/<you> (re-run flicker secrets diff to check drift)
mix phx.server         # reads .env automatically via config/runtime.exs
# or via ./bin/dev which loads .env via direnv
```

### Production (flicker)

A flicker app's environment is part of its app config — managed via the flicker API/CLI/UI. **Do not use `fly secrets`.** Update the app's flicker env, then redeploy. DB migrations run as part of the flicker deploy (the build's release step).

### Common required secrets

Most Phoenix projects need at minimum:
- `DATABASE_URL` — PostgreSQL connection string
- `SECRET_KEY_BASE` — `mix phx.gen.secret`
- `PHX_HOST` — hostname for URL generation

Optional depending on project:
- `TIGRIS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `TIGRIS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `TIGRIS_BUCKET_NAME` — S3 storage
- `ZULIP_URL`, `ZULIP_BOT_EMAIL`, `ZULIP_API_KEY` — `log_out` logging
- `RESEND_API_KEY` — email
- `GITHUB_TOKEN` — in-app bug reporter posting to GitHub Issues (FoodFeed)

## Git working discipline

Branch-first, commit-often, clean-merge. These prevent lost work — especially when more than one agent/session can touch the same repo.

1. **Worktree + branch before you edit — DEFAULT for any agent doing code changes.** A branch alone does NOT isolate the working tree: a branch is only a pointer, and a clone has ONE working folder + ONE HEAD, so a `checkout` in any session yanks files/HEAD out from under another and can interleave or discard its uncommitted edits. Any agent that will make code changes MUST work in its own `git worktree` — its own working directory with its own branch — not just a branch in the shared clone:
   ```bash
   git worktree add ../<repo>-<task> -b <branch>   # own dir + own branch, off the default branch
   ```
   Then do ALL work inside `../<repo>-<task>`. One constraint: the same branch can't be checked out in two worktrees at once (use a distinct branch per worktree). Everything else still works — the worktrees share the clone's `.git` object store, so fetches, commits, pushes, and PRs all behave exactly as in the main clone. Solo single-session work MAY stay in the main clone; but any time more than one agent/session may touch the same repo, the worktree is mandatory.
2. **Commit every chunk.** Commit after each logical unit of work; never accumulate substantial uncommitted changes. Uncommitted edits live only in the working tree and are **silently discarded if the branch is switched** (e.g. by a concurrent session). Committed work survives in git (recoverable via the reflog even if a branch moves). This is the backstop even when you're in your own worktree.
3. **Rebase, then clean-merge.** When the work is done, rebase the feature branch onto the latest default branch and resolve any conflicts there. Because you only ever stack new commits on top of the default branch, the merge is always a clean fast-forward — never a tangled merge.

> This section exists because an agent left a substantial refactor uncommitted while a concurrent session switched the branch in the same clone — silently wiping the work; in another incident two agent sessions worked in the same clone on different branches and one session's `checkout` moved the other off its branch and interleaved its uncommitted edits. A branch does not isolate the working tree — a worktree does. Worktree-per-agent + commit-often makes both impossible.

**Exception — live-read config/dotfile repos** (e.g. this `agent-workflow` repo): these are read directly from the working tree, so they commit straight to the default branch. The "feature branch behind a PR" rule is for code that deploys via CI, not for config you read in place.

## Task management

**Single tracker for everything = Flicker Tickets** (via the public `flicker` CLI/API). The phase/status model is the installed `flicker-workflow` skill (public mirror: go9/flicker-workflow); org overlay rules are in `~/Sites/agent-workflow/adapters/shared/workflow-core.md` — read both before any planning conversation.

**How it works:**
- Work lives as **Flicker tickets inside a Flicker Project**. (Ticket documents — not `.go9/artifacts/*` — carry plans, decisions, and handoffs; see "No-spontaneous-markdown rule" below.)
- Segment work by **Flicker Project**. Active projects of note: `flicker`; and `enventory`, which currently holds **skusync + enventory + cardhoard** work, segmented by title prefix/tag until native tags land.
- A ticket's **status** is one of the canonical values: `backlog` → `selected_for_dev` → `in_progress` → `done`. Named transitions: **select-for-dev**, **start**, **complete**, **reopen**, **defer**. Agents only pick up implementation from **`selected_for_dev`** (unless the user explicitly overrides). New work starts in `backlog`.
- **Move it on pickup and on finish — mandatory.** The moment you start implementing, run `flicker ticket start` to move the ticket to **`in_progress`** *before* writing code; when it's validated/merged, run `flicker ticket complete` to move it to **`done`** in the same step. A watched in-progress set is how we catch lingering work; skipping these transitions is what let already-built tickets rot in the backlog (see workflow-core → *Lifecycle discipline*).
- No implementation before an approved `task_contract` and `plan_consensus`; no push/deploy without explicit approval (see workflow-core).

Code still lives in GitHub repos: most under `orlando-umbrella` (wutdu, colculate, goscrape, two-pest-control, flicker, and the product apps); `log_out` and `livecode` under `go9`; the enventory side repos (enventory-ios, and AgentEye as `agenteye`) under the separate `Enventory` org — those use GitHub-hosted runners; `flicker-arc` is an orlando-umbrella-only pool. Tickets reference repos/PRs but live in Flicker, not GitHub.

### Pre-flight: ALWAYS search before planning

```bash
# Search existing tickets (the single tracker)
flicker ticket list --json                     # filter/grep by project, status, keyword
flicker memory search "<keywords>"             # durable history: prior tickets, decisions, events
```

Surface findings to the user BEFORE proposing anything new. If a relevant ticket already exists → extend it instead of duplicating (reuse before create).

### Ticket hygiene (mandatory)

A healthy backlog is part of the OS.

- **Reuse before create.** If a related ticket already captures the work, adopt it.
- **Update stale tickets.** If a ticket is directionally right but outdated, edit its title/body/document instead of filing a parallel replacement.
- **Split mis-scoped tickets.** If one ticket mixes unrelated work, keep the parent and spawn focused child tickets.
- **Close or supersede junk.** If a ticket is obsolete, duplicated, or replaced by a better one, close it (complete/defer with a short explanation) and link to the successor.
- **Do not leave planning debris behind.** Umbrella tickets, abandoned drafts, and duplicate child tickets must be merged, closed, or marked superseded before the session ends.
- **Planning should improve the tracker.** Every planning pass should leave Flicker Tickets cleaner and more trustworthy than it found it.

### No-spontaneous-markdown rule

**Agents MUST NOT create new markdown files on their own initiative.** Plans, decisions, status updates, analyses, and todos go to **Flicker Tickets** (ticket documents) — not new `.md` files.

Allowed without asking:
1. Editing existing markdown files
2. Markdown written by third-party skills (`superpowers:writing-plans` → `docs/superpowers/plans/`)
3. Required infrastructure files (`SKILL.md`, `plugin.json`)

Banned (route to Flicker Tickets instead):
- `DECISIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `NOTES.md`, `MIGRATION.md`, `REVIEW.md`, `TODO.md`, `BACKLOG.md`
- `docs/<feature>-plan.md` — plans are ticket documents, not files
- "Working tracker" / "Live checklist" markdown — that's a tracking ticket with a tasklist

**The principle:** user explicitly typing the filename = consent. Agent inferring "we should probably document this" = no consent — open a ticket.

## Elixir / Phoenix conventions

These apply to every Elixir/Phoenix codebase. Project CLAUDE.mds should NOT restate them.

The `elixir-phoenix-guide` plugin (14 skills) enforces additional rules via hooks; those skills must be invoked before writing `.ex`/`.exs`/`.heex` files.

### HTTP client

Use **`Req`** or **`Req.LLM`** only. Never `HTTPoison`, `Tesla`, or `httpc`.

### Icons

**Hero icons first, Font Awesome as backup.**

### Struct access

**Never use `get_in` or map access syntax** (`struct[:field]`) with structs. Use dot notation or pattern matching.

### No `defdelegate`

Write explicit wrapper functions instead. Easier to grep, easier to refactor.

### No grouped aliases

```elixir
# ❌ Bad
alias Enventory.{Sales, Products, Inventory}

# ✅ Good
alias Enventory.Sales
alias Enventory.Products
alias Enventory.Inventory
```

### No lingering scripts

Replace standalone scripts with reusable functions in proper modules.

### Large context refactoring

Contexts over **500 lines** should be split into sub-modules. See the `refactor-context` skill.

---

## lantern-ui quick reference

Always use lantern-ui semantic color tokens (the drop-in for the old Fluxon tokens) instead of hardcoded Tailwind colors.

**Text:** `text-foreground`, `text-foreground-soft`, `text-muted-foreground`
**Backgrounds:** `bg-card`, `bg-overlay`, `bg-primary`
**Borders:** `border-base`
**Semantic:** `text-danger`/`bg-danger`, `text-success`/`bg-success`, `text-warning`/`bg-warning`

See the `lantern-ui-components` skill for component patterns.

---

## Changelog discipline

Projects that deploy on push to main follow the "push = release" convention:

- `CHANGELOG.md` at the project root, [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com) format.
- `## [Unreleased]` section at the top — accumulate changes as you work.
- Before pushing to main, move `[Unreleased]` to a dated version section.

## Skills — where they come from, and the scope rule

Don't maintain a list of skill names here; it rots. (The list that used to live
in this section named eight skills, **all of which had ceased to exist** when it
was audited on 2026-07-28.) Run `/doctor`, or `ls ~/.claude/skills`, to see what
is actually installed. What you do need to know is which of four sources a
skill comes from, because that determines how it updates:

| Source | Installed by | Updated by |
|---|---|---|
| **Product** — `flicker-plan/implement/test/release/ship/recall` | `flicker skill install --workflow --all --global` | re-run after a CLI upgrade |
| **Org** — this repo's `skills/` | `agent-workflow/install` | `git pull` (Claude symlinks are live); re-run `./install` for Pi/Codex |
| **Third-party domain packs** — iOS/Swift etc. | `npx skills add <owner>/<repo>` **in the repo** | `npx skills update` |
| **flicker Agent Config** — the org's own library, assigned per project | `flicker harness install skill <path>` / `assign` | `flicker harness sync` in the repo; `flicker harness doctor` to verify |

### flicker Agent Config: the same skills, centrally owned

Agent config is a **flicker feature** (`flicker harness`), not a separate tool.
Rules, skills, and MCP specs live in one versioned org library, are assigned to
a cell of an owner × applies-to grid (`org | user` × `everywhere | one
project`), and `flicker harness sync` writes them into whichever harnesses a
working copy has. Two consequences worth knowing before you touch an adopted
repo:

- **`AGENTS.md` becomes a generated artifact** in a repo that ran
  `flicker harness import` — edit rules, re-sync, commit the render. A hand
  edit inside the managed block is reported and then overwritten.
- **Only Claude Code pickup is verified live.** The Codex, Pi, and opencode
  adapters write to each harness's documented path, but nothing has yet proven
  a live session in those three loads what was written.

This repo (`agent-workflow`) is NOT adopted — its `skills/` are still the org
source of truth, installed by `./install`. Product docs:
flickercloud.com/docs/agent-config.

### The scope rule: domain packs install per repo, never globally

A skill's *body* loads only when invoked, but its *name + description* are in
context in **every** session. That index is budgeted at **~3,000 tokens**
(raised from ~2,000 on 2026-08-02 — the legitimate org + product skill set
alone runs ~2,700, and a check that warns on the healthy baseline just trains
you to ignore it). Past the budget, descriptions are silently stripped — and a
skill with no description cannot be routed to, so it never fires.

This is not hypothetical. On 2026-07-28 the 84-skill iOS pack was installed
globally, putting the index at ~12,300 tokens (6× over). **50 skills had their
descriptions stripped; all 50 had zero lifetime uses** — invisible, not
unwanted. Rescoping the pack to the three iOS repos took every non-iOS session
from ~12,300 to ~2,449.

So: while you are over budget, **installing one skill can silently disable a
different one.** Global scope is a shared, oversubscribed resource. Put a domain
pack in the repos that need it (`npx skills add …`, no `-g`), commit the
lockfile, gitignore the installed dirs.

Full model, the per-type detection rule, and the current iOS set:
[`docs/REPO_STRUCTURE.md`](../../docs/REPO_STRUCTURE.md) → Layer 6.

# Workflow core (org overlay)

**The workflow contract itself is published and installed, not maintained here.**
Substance: the installed `flicker-workflow` skill (`flicker skill install --workflow
--global`) and its public mirror https://github.com/go9/flicker-workflow —
stages, canonical statuses/transitions, document kinds, CLI surface, hard rules,
and the PR + review loop all live there. This file carries only what is specific
to THIS org.

## Org rules on top of the contract

### Tracker rule (no coexistence)
**Flicker Tickets is the only tracker.** GitHub is code-only (branches, PRs, AI
PR review) — never tickets, plans, or status. Do not split one piece of active
work across two trackers.

### Lifecycle discipline (MANDATORY — keep the board honest)
On pickup → `flicker ticket start` *before* writing code. On finish →
`flicker ticket complete` in the same step. Why: a short, accurate in-progress
list is the single best signal of live work. The 2026-06 flicker audit found
**8 fully-built tickets still open**, invisible among ~50 — skipped transitions
are how completion hides.

### Project segmentation
One Flicker Project per product. Shared projects (e.g. `enventory` holds
skusync / enventory / cardhoard work) segment by title prefix or tags until
native tags ship.

### Reviewer + danger zones (org instantiation)
The pluggable reviewer on product repos is self-hosted PR-Agent; `flicker` also
runs the Claude Review action. flicker-ship danger zones for this org: SNI
proxy, K8s data-plane adapter core, billing/money paths, DB migrations.

### Code intelligence policy
Serena MCP first for code navigation/search/reference tracing; shell search only
when Serena is unavailable or the task is raw text/log processing. RTK is an
output-optimization layer, never the first choice for code intelligence.

### Worktree rule (restated because it prevents lost work)
Any agent making code changes works in a dedicated worktree + branch
(`git worktree add ../<repo>-<ticket> -b <branch>`) — a branch alone does not
isolate the working tree. See conventions → "Git working discipline".

## Infrastructure: flicker prod host

Hosting details live in `agent-workflow/projects/flicker/CLAUDE.md`; read it
before any operation on the production host. The data plane is a Kubernetes
cell (RKE2 + OpenEBS-ZFS + CNPG). For Proxmox/VM-level emergency operations,
read `agent-workflow/docs/proxmox-homelab-runbook.md`.

## Workflow = Flicker Tickets

The tracker is **Flicker Tickets** (the portfolio's GitHub Issues were migrated into
Flicker Tickets in 2026-06). GitHub is still used for **code**: branches, PRs, and
review (self-hosted PR-Agent + the Claude review action). It is no longer used for tickets/planning.

## Claude command mapping

Primary top-level workflow (Flicker-native):
- `/flicker-plan <idea|bug|project>` -> planning ending in tickets, task contract, and plan consensus
- `/flicker-implement <ticket>` -> code changes only after approved task contract + approved plan consensus + selected for dev
- `/flicker-test <ticket|PR>` -> review + QA + regression + test verdict
- `/flicker-release <ticket>` -> merge/deploy readiness only; explicit approval still required
- `/flicker-ship <ticket>` -> autonomous pickup -> implement -> PR -> review-until-clean -> merge, within safety rails (tests green; danger zones escalate to a human)
- `/flicker-recall <query>` -> search ticket documents + project memory

**The workflow skills are NOT in this repo** — they ship with the flicker CLI. All of
these follow the shared contract in the installed `flicker-workflow` skill (public
mirror: https://github.com/go9/flicker-workflow) and use the public
`flicker` CLI/API for tickets/memory plus `gh` for the PR/review loop.

Setup once per machine (REQUIRED — the skills don't exist until installed):

```bash
flicker auth login <api-key>
flicker project use <slug>              # e.g. enventory
flicker skill install --workflow --global   # installs flicker-plan … flicker-recall + the contract
```

Doctor check: `~/.claude/skills/flicker-plan/SKILL.md` must exist. If `/flicker-plan`
is unavailable in a session, run the install command above — do not hunt for the
skills in this repo; they moved into the CLI (flicker #746).

## Claude tool priority

- Prefer Serena MCP for code navigation/search/edit planning before Bash, Grep, `rg`, `find`, or RTK-wrapped shell commands.
- If Serena is not connected, first try to connect/enable Serena MCP; only then fall back to shell search.
- Treat RTK as a shell fallback/output-filtering layer only. RTK must not be the first choice for code intelligence.

This file keeps Claude from drifting off the Flicker workflow. The workflow
substance is NOT here — it ships with the flicker CLI: `flicker skill install
--workflow --global` (verify `~/.claude/skills/flicker-plan/SKILL.md` exists;
public mirror https://github.com/go9/flicker-workflow). When running any stage,

The tracker is **Flicker Tickets**, driven by the public `flicker` CLI/API.
GitHub is code-only — never look work up on GitHub Issues or reach for a
GitHub-Issues workflow.

Primary top-level stages (each is an installed skill):

1. `plan`      (`/flicker-plan`)
2. `implement` (`/flicker-implement`)
3. `test`      (`/flicker-test`)
4. `release`   (`/flicker-release`)

Plus `/flicker-ship` (autonomous end-to-end) and `/flicker-recall` (search
docs/memory). Do not invent alternate stage names unless the user explicitly
asks for internals.

## Claude-specific discipline

- Treat the workflow as a strict contract, not a loose suggestion.
- The gates are ambient, not just in-skill: no implementation before an approved
  `task_contract` + `plan_consensus`; agents pick up only `selected_for_dev`
  work; `flicker ticket start` before code, `complete` on merge; no
  push/deploy/merge without explicit current-turn approval.
- UI/product work requires a `design` document before execution readiness.
- When in doubt, preserve the ticket truth, the document chain, and approval gates.
- Keep the `ponytail` skill active by default (minimal-first, **full** intensity;

  solution and scope that actually works — across every stage, planning included.

# Orlando org conventions (core)

Org-wide rules for all agents and contributors, on every repo in the
orlando-umbrella portfolio. Installed per machine by `agent-workflow/install`;
source of truth: `orlando-umbrella/agent-workflow` → `skills/org-conventions.md`.

## Start here, every repo

- Read the repo's `AGENTS.md` first — it is the authoritative project
  instruction file (object model, commands, gotchas). The portfolio structure
  standard lives in `agent-workflow/docs/REPO_STRUCTURE.md`.
- **In a repo adopted into flicker Agent Config, `AGENTS.md` is a GENERATED
  artifact — edit the rules, not the file.** Adoption is visible in the file
  itself: a `<!-- BEGIN flicker rules … -->` marker means `flicker harness sync`
  re-renders that block, and a hand edit inside it is reported as somebody's
  work about to be overwritten. Change it with `flicker harness rule add` /
  `flicker harness sync` and commit the render. No marker = the repo was never
  imported and its `AGENTS.md` is hand-written as before. Product docs:
  flickercloud.com/docs/agent-config.
- The tracker for ALL work is **Flicker Tickets** (`flicker` CLI). GitHub is
  code-only: branches, PRs, review — never tickets, plans, or status docs.
- Workflow skills ship with the flicker CLI. Bootstrap once per machine:
  `flicker skill install --workflow --global`, then drive work with
  `/flicker-plan`, `/flicker-implement`, `/flicker-test`, `/flicker-release`.

## Ticket lifecycle (mandatory)

- Pick up implementation only from `selected_for_dev` (unless explicitly told).
- `flicker ticket start <id>` BEFORE writing code; `flicker ticket complete`
  when the work is validated/merged — same step, never later.
- Plans, decisions, status, reviews → ticket documents and memory. Do NOT
  create new markdown files for them in code repos.

## Git safety (these rules exist because work was lost)

- Any agent making code changes works in its own worktree + branch:
  `git worktree add ../<repo>-<task> -b <branch>`. A branch alone does not
  isolate the working tree; never switch branches in a shared checkout.
- Commit early and often. Never run destructive git commands (`restore`,
  `reset`, `checkout`) over uncommitted changes — `git status` first, commit
  or ask.
- **Never deploy without explicit, current approval.** On the product apps a
  deploy is an explicit `git push origin origin/main:deployed` (iOS:
  `test-flight`) — merging to `main` ships nothing and needs no deploy
  approval. "Commit" does not mean "push". Batch merges freely, then ship one
  deploy.

## Build stance: minimal-first

Default to the smallest solution that actually works: reuse what exists →
stdlib → platform feature → existing dep → only then new code. Root-cause
fixes over per-caller patches. Never simplify away correctness, tests,
validation at trust boundaries, security, or accessibility. Applies to
planning too: smallest ticket that solves the real need.

## Code conventions (Elixir/Phoenix repos)

- HTTP client: `Req` only (never HTTPoison/Tesla/httpc).
- No `defdelegate`; no grouped aliases (`alias App.{A, B}`); no struct access
  via `struct[:field]` — use dot notation or pattern matching.
- Heroicons first; semantic color tokens, not hardcoded Tailwind colors.
- No lingering one-off scripts — promote to functions in proper modules.

## Honesty in public surfaces

When changing behavior (deploys, proxy, mail, secrets, backups, CLI), update
the matching public claim surface (landing/docs/security/legal) in the same
PR. Marketing copy must describe what the code actually does.

## CRITICAL: Git Workflow Rules — NEVER VIOLATE THESE

**YOU MUST FOLLOW THESE RULES AT ALL TIMES:**

1. **COMMIT EARLY AND OFTEN**: Commit changes in logical chunks as you work. DO NOT accumulate large amounts of uncommitted changes.

2. **NEVER DELETE UNCOMMITTED WORK**: Before running ANY destructive git command (`git restore`, `git reset`, `git checkout`, etc.), you MUST:
   - First run `git status` to check for uncommitted changes
   - If there are uncommitted changes, COMMIT them first
   - NEVER run `git restore` or similar commands on files with uncommitted changes
   - If you must discard changes, ask the user first

3. **COMMIT BEFORE SWITCHING TASKS**: Before switching to work on a different project or task, commit all current work.

4. **VERIFY BEFORE DESTRUCTIVE OPERATIONS**: Before any git command that could lose work:
   - Run `git status` and `git diff` to see what will be lost
   - Ask the user for confirmation if there are uncommitted changes
   - Consider creating a backup commit or stash

5. **WHEN IN DOUBT, COMMIT**: If you're unsure whether to commit, ALWAYS commit. Small, frequent commits are better than lost work.

6. **NEVER DEPLOY WITHOUT EXPLICIT USER CONFIRMATION.** A deploy costs real CI minutes or money and puts code in front of customers. Default behavior: **commit, then stop**. The user will say "push", "deploy", or "ship it" when they want it shipped. If only "commit" is requested, **do not push, even if the work feels finished**.

   **What counts as a deploy depends on the repo — know which model you're in:**

   *Explicit-deploy repos (a branch push is the deploy; merging to `main` ships NOTHING):*
   - `flicker`, `foodfeed`, `enventory-new`, `skusync`, `goprint-registry`, `agenteye` — deploy is `git push origin origin/main:deployed`
   - `cardhoard-ios` — deploy is `git push origin origin/main:test-flight` (Xcode Cloud → TestFlight)

   In these repos, **merging a PR to `main` is safe and needs no deploy approval** — it ships nothing. The gated act is the push to `deployed`/`test-flight`. Batch as many merges as you like, then ship one deploy.

   Useful consequences: `git log deployed..main` is exactly the unreleased set, `deployed` is a durable record of what is actually in production, and rollback is `git push -f origin <good-sha>:deployed`.

   (App hosting moved off Fly.io to flicker — see agent-workflow conventions → Deployment standards. Don't use `fly deploy` / `fly secrets`.)

   **Still on push-to-main auto-deploy — treat the push to `main` itself as the gated act:**
   - `foodfeed-ios` — every merge to `main` triggers an Xcode Cloud TestFlight build. Moving it to a `test-flight` branch like cardhoard's requires editing the workflow's branch condition in **App Store Connect**, not in the repo, so it can't be changed from here.

   For these, batch related commits — one push of three commits is one deploy; three pushes of one commit each is three deploys.

**Rules 2–5 exist because uncommitted work was accidentally deleted with `git restore`, causing hours of lost work. Rule 6 exists because Claude burned through CI minutes on multiple unconfirmed pushes during a single session. These must NEVER happen again.**

> The explicit-deploy model was adopted 2026-08-03, after a session where merge-and-deploy being the same act meant three ready PRs had to be staged one at a time around an unrelated deploy failure. Separating them is what makes "merge freely, deploy deliberately" possible.

## RTK — Rust Token Killer

Token-optimized CLI proxy (60–90% savings on dev operations). All standard CLI calls (git, npm, etc.) are auto-rewritten via the Claude Code hook to use `rtk <cmd>` transparently. Meta commands:

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

If `rtk gain` fails with "command not found", verify the right binary is on PATH (`which rtk`) — name collision with `reachingforthejack/rtk` (Rust Type Kit) is a known foot-gun.

# RTK - Rust Token Killer

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

## Meta Commands (always use rtk directly)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics
rtk gain --history    # Show command usage history with savings
rtk discover          # Analyze Claude Code history for missed opportunities
rtk proxy <cmd>       # Execute raw command without filtering (for debugging)
```

## Installation Verification

```bash
rtk --version         # Should show: rtk X.Y.Z
rtk gain              # Should work (not "command not found")
which rtk             # Verify correct binary
```

⚠️ **Name collision**: If `rtk gain` fails, you may have reachingforthejack/rtk (Rust Type Kit) installed instead.

All other commands are automatically rewritten by the Claude Code hook.
Example: `git status` → `rtk git status` (transparent, 0 tokens overhead)
